absent: Full enable, disable, bypass and error-recovery state machine beyond the queued-work tail shown
Layouts and valid ranges for scheduler operations flags and numeric tuning constants
Structure layouts for scheduler instance, persistent shard, capability mask and run-queue sync entries

findings.text: Enabling idle handling adapts two global switches to the loaded operations: the builtin idle path stays active when no custom idle hook exists or when a keep-builtin flag is set, and a per-node variant follows its own flag. After adjusting the switches the routine empties the idle tracking sets so later idle transitions repopulate them.

Idle tracking starts empty to favor safety over completeness. When per-node tracking is off only the global set is emptied, otherwise every node set is emptied. Both the CPU and SMT views are cleared. The design accepts briefly missing an idle CPU while guaranteeing a busy CPU is never reported idle.

Scheduler activation rejects machines with boot domain isolation, then lazily creates a single FIFO helper worker under a dedicated mutex with double-checked publication. It selects root or sub-scheduler startup work based on build option and cgroup identity, queues the work on the helper, waits for completion, and returns the work result.

The tail of root activation reports a numeric failure status through the scheduler error path, ensures pending disable work is drained, and forces the command result to a neutral zero so the caller does not propagate the internal code further.

Persistent shard allocation is a no-op returning success when the scheduler is not a CID type or lacks an arena pool. Otherwise it reads the global shard-to-node table under enable-mutex protection, allocates one persistent shard per CID shard with node affinity, releases all partial results on any failure with an out-of-memory status, records the count, issues an ordering barrier, and publishes the array with a single ordered store.

Each persistent shard carries its owning scheduler link, base CID and count taken from the global range table, per-capability masks initialized to its range, plus a caps-updated tracker with its own lock, pending list, in-memory mask sized for the shard, and an arena-backed mask also initialized to the range. Allocation is node-local with zeroed memory, lock initialization precedes use, and arena backing failure destroys the whole shard.

Root capability initialization marks every capability mask on every persistent shard as fully allowed. When sub-scheduler support is compiled out the header provides inline replacements for allocation and initialization that immediately report success or do nothing.

Rescue tuning derives bandwidth and quantum from operations with built-in defaults, disables rescue when a sentinel is configured, converts quantum to nanoseconds with a tick floor, derives saturation delta and funding period by scaled division, clamps the overload threshold between min and max millisecond bounds with halflife at one quarter, warns when one funding period exceeds half the overload threshold, and separately warns when the watchdog timeout does not exceed the overload threshold. A header fallback provides an empty implementation when the feature is disabled.

Stale capability sync cleanup walks every possible CPU, acquires each run queue with an interrupt-saving scoped guard, and discards queued sync entries before releasing. A header fallback provides an empty version when the feature is disabled.

Program context access permits only reads within the fixed argument area with proper alignment and delegates to generic context checking. Field access to task state is narrow: the common helper exposes only the disallow field of the cached task type, the standard hook additionally exposes slice and dispatch virtual time, while the CID hook exposes only the common subset and denies everything else.

Copying user-provided operations into kernel memory validates each field by offset: batch size bounded, flags masked against the full set, name copied and required non-empty, timeout converted and bounded, dump length defaulted when zero, hotplug and shard size copied directly, rescue bandwidth and quantum range-checked with sentinel handling and minimum enforcement, and sub-scheduler identity copied when enabled. Unknown offsets fall through to default handling.

Operation registration rejects sleepable programs except for a lifecycle allowlist covering task init, cgroup management, CPU online and offline, CID init, scheduler init and exit, and sub-scheduler attach and detach. When sub-schedulers are enabled, dispatch and capability-update callbacks request a private stack with dedicated recursion detection.

Normal registration builds an enable command from the operations and delegates to the shared enable path. CID registration first scans all attached programs for arena use, fails if more than one arena appears or none appears on capable builds, holds a reference on the single arena, passes it to enable, and releases it if not consumed. Unregistration disables with an unregister reason, drains disable work, clears the private pointer, and drops the scheduler reference. Update always reports unsupported, validation always succeeds, and init caches the task type identifier.

Two verifier configurations share the same context access and function prototype helpers but differ in field-access policy for standard versus CID schedulers. The outer operations descriptor links those verifiers with registration, validation, member copy and check, lifecycle hooks, a fixed type name, module ownership, and a table of default stub implementations used for control-flow integrity.

The default core scheduling callbacks are inert: selection and task creation signal rejection, yielding and core ordering signal negative, and queueing, dispatch, timing, state transitions, weight, affinity, idle notification, CPU handover, task teardown and task enable or disable perform no action and retain no state.
Default cgroup callbacks are inert with creation and move preparation signaling rejection while exit, movement commit and cancel, weight, bandwidth and idle adjustments perform no action.
Default hierarchy and lifecycle callbacks are inert: attach, CID setup and scheduler setup signal rejection, while detach, CPU online and offline, exit and all diagnostic dumps perform no action.

Partial construction never leaks: shard array build frees earlier shards and the array on failure, single shard build destroys itself when arena backing is unavailable, helper creation failure returns out-of-memory without publishing, CID setup with inconsistent or missing arena aborts before enable, and oversized or unknown-flagged operation fields abort member copy with size or argument errors.
